source_first_seen.unit_name: From long recordings to windowed labels
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The proposed labeling scheme turns each long recording into multiple short windows and marks a window positive only when it ends right after the speaker finishes "Robert, turn on" [ts=1661s] [ts=1776s]. This turns roughly 100 long clips into around 3,000 binary examples, which is operationally convenient for training a classifier [ts=1775s] [ts=1798s]. The first model then reports 97% accuracy while producing zero detections, revealing that the dataset is so skewed that always predicting the negative class looks strong under the naive metric [ts=1813s] [ts=1860s]. The segment uses this to motivate rebalancing strategies rather than trusting headline accuracy alone [ts=1914s] [ts=1978s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Balancing data, fighting overfitting, and building robustness
target_first_seen.unit_summary: After the imbalance fix, the next observed failure is a train/dev gap: the model does well on train but only about 50% on the dev set, which the lecture interprets as overfitting and a cue to try regularization or more data [ts=2260s] [ts=2411s]. The instructor then describes a synthetic augmentation trick that works in speech: add clean trigger utterances to background-noise recordings so the summed waveform simulates speech in realistic environments [ts=2495s] [ts=2583s]. He warns that using only trigger phrases would teach voice activity detection rather than phrase recognition, so negative examples must also include other spoken content [ts=2608s] [ts=2664s]. The segment closes with a rule of thumb that richer and more diverse training data usually wins, provided the model has enough capacity to absorb that diversity [ts=2803s] [ts=2858s].

source_first_seen.unit_summary: Ng opens by explaining the flipped format and asks students to use live class time for richer questioning rather than passive replay of recorded content [ts=35s] [ts=88s]. He motivates the subject by contrasting older ML methods that plateau with more data against neural networks that continue improving as size, data, and compute scale [ts=198s] [ts=276s]. target_first_seen.unit_name: Implementation consistency, contamination, and keeping test sets alive
target_first_seen.unit_summary: This segment argues that even apparently simple benchmarks can be unstable. For multiple-choice tasks, changing how answers are formatted can change generations and model rankings, and MMLU historically had multiple incompatible implementations that differed in prompting and answer-selection procedures such as constrained decoding versus token or log-likelihood scoring [ts=3840s] [ts=3878s] [ts=3916s]. Yann then moves to contamination: benchmark scores can be inflated when test data or close variants appear in pretraining, illustrated by code-benchmark anecdotes where GPT-4 did very well on older Codeforces problems but failed on newer ones [ts=4032s] [ts=4063s]. The lecture separates contamination from broader overfitting to public test sets, then suggests mitigations including private or regenerated test sets such as GSM1K, dynamic test sets such as Dynabench, and leakage detection heuristics such as unusually confident answers or sensitivity to the original order of examples [ts=4153s] [ts=4197s] [ts=4223s].

p5_trace.keep_rationale: Capability benchmark contamination is one external evaluation risk inside frontier-model diagnostics.

target_first_seen.unit_name: CNN saliency maps and integrated gradients
target_first_seen.unit_summary: For the zoo classifier case, the lecture first motivates explanations that show whether a model is looking at the relevant image region rather than merely outputting a class probability [ts=891s] [ts=1053s]. A saliency map is built by differentiating a class score such as dog with respect to the input pixels, so bright pixels are the ones whose perturbation most affects the score [ts=1212s] [ts=1259s]. The instructor emphasizes using the pre-softmax class score rather than the post-softmax probability because post-softmax depends on all competing class scores [ts=1280s] [ts=1315s]. Integrated gradients are presented as a more common extension that accumulates gradients along a path from a black baseline image to the actual image, with a retina-lesion example showing attribution concentrated near the annotated lesion [ts=1416s] [ts=1467s].

source_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 9: What Is Going On Inside My Model?
source_first_seen.unit_name: Occlusion sensitivity and class activation maps
source_first_seen.unit_summary: Occlusion sensitivity replaces a moving region of the image with a gray or dark square and measures how the true-class score changes as the square moves [ts=1524s] [ts=1557s]. If occluding the dog face drops the Pomeranian probability, or occluding a wheel drops the car-wheel probability, the method supports the claim that the model is relying on semantically relevant regions [ts=1608s] [ts=1657s]. The class activation map section targets real-time visualization: the lecture identifies fully connected layers after flattening as the part that mixes away localization, then replaces most of that head with global average pooling plus a final fully connected layer [ts=1725s] [ts=1834s] [ts=1893s]. A CAM is then formed as a weighted combination of last-convolution feature maps for a selected class, producing a heatmap that can be overlaid on the input [ts=1973s] [ts=2054s].

He motivates the topic by noting that modern language models are enormous deep systems, then reviews how backprop enabled hidden-layer neural nets in the 1980s and 1990s but deeper networks were long believed too hard to train until late-2000s and 2010s ideas reversed that stagnation [ts=177s] [ts=354s] [ts=422s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Neuroscience and early computer vision foundations
target_first_seen.unit_summary: This segment begins with Hubel and Wiesel's 1959 experiments on mammalian vision, emphasizing two principles: neurons in early visual cortex have local receptive fields and respond to simple oriented patterns, and visual processing is hierarchical, with increasingly complex features built from simpler ones [ts=485s] [ts=600s]. Li explicitly notes that this perspective profoundly influenced neural network modeling for vision [ts=623s]. The lecture then introduces Larry Roberts' 1963 work on shape as an early PhD thesis in computer vision and places it alongside the optimistic 1966 MIT summer vision project as landmarks in the field's origin [ts=666s] [ts=769s]. David Marr's 1970s framework is presented as a staged pipeline from input image to primal sketch, 2.5D sketch, and ultimately 3D representation [ts=773s] [ts=847s]. Li pauses to explain that recovering 3D structure from 2D measurements is fundamentally ill-posed, which is why nature uses multiple eyes and correspondence, yet even humans do not recover perfect geometry [ts=880s] [ts=958s]. She contrasts vision with language by arguing that language is generated and sequential, while vision must model a real physical world governed by physics and materials [ts=968s] [ts=1018s].

p5_trace.keep_rationale: Kept because deep learning resurgence from data, compute, and scale is treated as prerequisite machinery before classical computer vision and hand-crafted features becomes the main idea in one unit, though the dependency is evidenced only once.

rationale: Autoregressive language modeling is a foundational generation mechanism; open-ended generation/evaluation is not prerequisite machinery for next-token modeling.

source_first_seen.unit_name: What NLG is and how tasks vary by open-endedness
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The segment defines natural language generation as NLP where the output is natural language, contrasting it with understanding tasks whose input is language [ts=155s]. It notes a historical shift from rule-based templates and infilling to deep learning systems [ts=189s]. The lecture then surveys examples including machine translation, digital assistants, summarization, creative story writing, data-to-text, image captioning, and ChatGPT as a general-purpose NLG system [ts=214s] [ts=280s]. It organizes tasks by open-endedness: translation and summarization have relatively constrained output spaces, dialogue allows multiple valid continuations, and story generation has extremely large valid output space [ts=348s] [ts=432s]. The segment closes by formalizing this spectrum with entropy, arguing that high-entropy tasks are more open-ended and that this distinction will matter for both decoding and training choices [ts=493s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Language models and n-gram fundamentals
target_first_seen.unit_summary: A language model is defined as a system that assigns a probability distribution to the next token given the previous context, and equivalently as a model that assigns probability to an entire sequence via a chain-rule decomposition into next-token conditionals [ts=1714s] [ts=1777s] [ts=1821s]. The lecture stresses that language models long predate ChatGPT and underlie autocomplete and query suggestion systems [ts=1862s] [ts=1882s] [ts=1928s]. It then introduces n-gram language models, where a Markov assumption keeps only the most recent n-1 words and predicts the next word from relative frequencies of observed short contexts [ts=1975s] [ts=2106s] [ts=2157s].

p5_trace.keep_rationale: Kept because open-ended generation and evaluation is treated as prerequisite machinery before autoregressive language modeling becomes the main idea in one unit, though the dependency is evidenced only once.

source_first_seen.unit_name: Limitations of supervised fine-tuning
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The instructor summarizes instruction fine-tuning as simple, then lists why it is not enough [ts=2043s] [ts=2068s]. It depends on expensive human demonstrations, especially for specialized questions that may require high expertise [ts=2076s] [ts=2098s]. Many open-ended or creative tasks do not have a single correct answer [ts=2116s] [ts=2125s]. Token-level language modeling loss also treats mistakes too uniformly: calling Avatar an adventure show and calling it a musical can be penalized similarly despite very different semantic severity [ts=2135s] [ts=2164s]. Another issue is that human-written answers may become a bottleneck as models generate better answers than labelers [ts=2169s] [ts=2192s]. The main conceptual problem is objective mismatch: the desired goal is outputs humans prefer, but SFT still performs next-token prediction on curated data [ts=2215s] [ts=2238s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Exposure bias, alternative training schemes, and RLHF context
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The lecture revisits repetition from the training side and argues that maximum-likelihood language models can assign high probability to bad degenerate strings [ts=2473s]. The core diagnosis is exposure bias: under teacher forcing the model trains on gold prefixes, but at generation time it must condition on its own imperfect outputs, creating a harmful train-test mismatch [ts=2510s] [ts=2541s]. Scheduled sampling narrows this gap by mixing model-generated and gold tokens with a probability that increases through training, though the objective can be unstable [ts=2560s]. DAgger similarly augments training data with model-generated sequences so the model learns on states it will actually encounter [ts=2603s]. The lecture also presents retrieval-augmented generation, where the model begins from a retrieved prototype and edits it by insertion, deletion, or swapping, reducing exposure bias because generation no longer starts from scratch left-to-right [ts=2655s]. Reinforcement learning is then framed as an MDP over states, actions, policies, and rewards, with rewards derived from automatic metrics or human preference [ts=2693s] [ts=2827s]. The lecture warns that optimizing BLEU or ROUGE can game the metric rather than improve true quality [ts=2744s]. It finishes with the modern pipeline behind ChatGPT-style systems: large-scale pretraining, instruction tuning, and then RLHF, with RLHF viewed as difficult from scratch but effective on top of a strong pretrained model [ts=3110s] [ts=3130s].

p5_trace.keep_rationale: RLHF over text generation uses reward models trained from human preference comparisons.

rationale: Occlusion sensitivity is a perturbation attribution method and does not require gradient saliency as prerequisite machinery.

source_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 9: What Is Going On Inside My Model?
source_first_seen.unit_name: CNN saliency maps and integrated gradients
source_first_seen.unit_summary: For the zoo classifier case, the lecture first motivates explanations that show whether a model is looking at the relevant image region rather than merely outputting a class probability [ts=891s] [ts=1053s]. A saliency map is built by differentiating a class score such as dog with respect to the input pixels, so bright pixels are the ones whose perturbation most affects the score [ts=1212s] [ts=1259s]. The instructor emphasizes using the pre-softmax class score rather than the post-softmax probability because post-softmax depends on all competing class scores [ts=1280s] [ts=1315s]. Integrated gradients are presented as a more common extension that accumulates gradients along a path from a black baseline image to the actual image, with a retina-lesion example showing attribution concentrated near the annotated lesion [ts=1416s] [ts=1467s].

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 9: What Is Going On Inside My Model?
target_first_seen.unit_name: Occlusion sensitivity and class activation maps
target_first_seen.unit_summary: Occlusion sensitivity replaces a moving region of the image with a gray or dark square and measures how the true-class score changes as the square moves [ts=1524s] [ts=1557s]. If occluding the dog face drops the Pomeranian probability, or occluding a wheel drops the car-wheel probability, the method supports the claim that the model is relying on semantically relevant regions [ts=1608s] [ts=1657s]. The class activation map section targets real-time visualization: the lecture identifies fully connected layers after flattening as the part that mixes away localization, then replaces most of that head with global average pooling plus a final fully connected layer [ts=1725s] [ts=1834s] [ts=1893s]. A CAM is then formed as a weighted combination of last-convolution feature maps for a selected class, producing a heatmap that can be overlaid on the input [ts=1973s] [ts=2054s].

p5_trace.keep_rationale: Occlusion sensitivity is an alternative image attribution method after saliency is introduced.

rationale: Activation functions appear in neural-network training, but they are not required to understand the general optimization procedure of gradient descent or SGD.
Activation-memory bottlenecks explain one practical fine-tuning constraint, but they are not a conceptual prerequisite for PEFT itself, which is primarily about updating fewer parameters.
Computation graphs are useful background for autograd, but neural-network module composition is an API/design abstraction and does not conceptually depend on graph formalism.
Computation graphs and regularization/generalization are both training topics, but regularization theory does not depend on computational-graph mechanics.
This is course framing rather than a reusable conceptual prerequisite edge; the class scope and the curriculum overview should not create a technical dependency.
The deep-learning resurgence provides historical context, but dynamic multi-actor activity understanding is an open application problem rather than a concept that depends on that resurgence framing.
Human recognition findings are cognitive/scientific motivation, not a conceptual successor that requires understanding the deep-learning resurgence.
Scene graphs and relational perception are related to vision progress, but the deep-learning-resurgence framing is not required to understand their object-relation representation.
Dynamic video activity understanding and perception-action integration are adjacent vision/robotics themes, but neither supplies prerequisite machinery for the other.
FSDP and activation checkpointing are separate memory-saving techniques; FSDP is not needed to understand checkpointing's recompute-for-memory tradeoff.
Implicit geometry is related to neural fields, but 3D Gaussian splatting is a distinct explicit/sparse primitive representation and does not require the implicit-function concept as a prerequisite.
Level sets and voxels are representation choices, while datasets and task space are broader context; the edge is topical rather than prerequisite.
Momentum and RMSProp are sibling optimizer ideas; RMSProp's adaptive squared-gradient scaling does not require momentum as a prerequisite.
Parametric surfaces are useful geometry background, but PointNet's key prerequisite is permutation-invariant set processing rather than parametric surface representation.
Small-filter receptive-field design and residual connections are both CNN architecture ideas, but residual identity skips do not conceptually require the small-filter design principle.
The source already includes NumPy-style slicing/indexing and shape manipulation, so the target is substantially overlapping rather than a separate prerequisite concept.

Tensor shape and broadcasting vocabulary is the prerequisite for reshaping/indexing, not the reverse; the reverse direction is already represented by the separate tensor-shapes-to-reshaping candidate.
ViT patch tokenization is not prerequisite machinery for CAM or Grad-CAM, which are class-evidence visualization methods centered on feature maps and gradients.
Saliency via input gradients depends on gradients and model inputs, not specifically on ViT patch tokenization or positional encoding.
